title: Dosage and styles
subtitle: Sweetness and categories
objectives: Explain non-vintage, vintage and prestige cuvée

steps.title: Dosage
steps.body: Dosage, added after disgorgement, sets the sweetness. Brut Nature: 0 to 3 g/l, no sugar added. Extra Brut: up to 6. Brut, the most common: up to 12. Extra Dry: 12 to 17. Sec: 17 to 32. Demi-Sec: 32 to 50. Doux: over 50. Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, a common confusion.

steps.title: Categories
steps.body: Non-vintage, NV, blends several years for consistency, about 80% of production. Vintage comes from one exceptional year, aged at least 3 years. Prestige cuvées, like Dom Pérignon, Cristal or Krug Grande Cuvée, are a house's top wine. Rosé is made by blending a little still red wine, unusually allowed in Champagne, or by saignée.

steps.prompt: Order these Champagne styles from driest to sweetest.
steps.explanation: Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut.

steps.title: Reading age
steps.body: Many producers now print the disgorgement date. A recently disgorged wine is fresher; one disgorged years ago has developed more toast and nuttiness. Some houses, like Bollinger with its R.D., release wines disgorged after very long lees ageing.

steps.prompt: How is most rosé Champagne made?
options: By blending in a little still red wine
steps.explanation: Champagne is an exception that allows blending red into white.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Dosage terms run from Brut Nature to Doux
NV, vintage and prestige cuvée are the main categories
Rosé Champagne is usually blended with red wine
